#2730. Valkyries parade historic WNBA title through ‘global capital of women’s sports’

On a sun-soaked, picture-perfect Bay Area day, the Golden State Valkyries did more than just parade a historic WNBA championship through the streets of San Francisco on Wednesday afternoon. In the words of Mayor Daniel Lurie, they established the city as the "global capital of women's sports."

And as Vakyries center Kiah Stokes said to NBC Bay Area's camera after stepping off the ferry Wednesday afternoon, they're just getting started.

"It's unreal," Oakland-born singer Kehlani told NBC Bay Area during the parade broadcast. "I feel like we deserved this for so long, we deserved a team, we deserved a women's team. And you see how people show up when you give us what we want and what we deserve."

While Bay Area sports fans may have waited more than two decades to finally get a WNBA team to call their own, it took just two seasons for the Valkyries to obtain what many thought was unobtainable for a team famously without a "star."

The Valkyries defeated the Atlanta Dream 68-63 on Saturday in the league's first finals Game 7. In doing so, they became the first expansion team, men's or women's, in any major North American sport to win a championship that fast.

Four days later, fans came out in droves to celebrate the title, cashing in on their very legitimate "Parade Time Off" from work and school to pack the Embarcadero with purple.

"Who knew a $25 (season ticket) deposit would go this far?" one fan told an NBC reporter.

After a tipoff ceremony and private party at 10 a.m., the Valkyries took a ferry across the water from Jack London Square in Oakland, Calif., to San Francisco. As the players disembarked, they were met by a frenzied crowd thousands deep.

"We love you guys — keep fighting," Natalie Nakase told an NBC reporter before hopping onto a bus to start the parade. "Do whatever looks impossible. DO IT!"

A WNBA champion four of the last five seasons, Stokes set a league record with 19 blocks in a finals defined by defense.

On Wednesday, she wore a shirt with a graphic from ESPN Analytics, ranking five WNBA teams by Basketball Power Index in order of most to least likely to win the finals. The Indiana Fever, bounced in the first round by the third-seeded Las Vegas Aces, were favored at 24 percent. The Valkyries weren't even on the list.

Instead of boarding the designated double-decker bus after getting off the ferry, finals MVP Gabby Williams took off down the Embarcadero, trophy in hand. She made her way to Mission Street, where the iconic drum that ushers in every Valkyries game at Chase Center was waiting to kick off the parade.

Williams, Lurie, and team emcee Ari Waller beat the drum for the last time in their iconic season to the rhythm of a resounding "G! S! V!" to get the party started.

The 1.2-mile route started at the Ferry Building and traveled south along the Embarcadero toward Oracle Park, home of the San Francisco Giants. Fans were supposed to gather behind the barricade on the water side of the Embarcadero, but so many people came that the other side of the street was packed as well.

Valkyries owners Peter Guber and Joe Lacob, who made good on their promise to deliver a championship within five years, were driven in classic cars, and San Francisco congresswoman Nancy Pelosi rode in a bus with a cable car-shaped chassis.

Whistles were blown. Smeezes and thizzles were hit. Rapper P-Lo sat on the back of a lowrider telling reporters about running the New York City Marathon in a Valkyries jersey, while LaRussell got off his float to rap multiple times. Giants mascot Lou Seal rode a Segway down the Embarcadero's bike lane, high-fiving fans with his fuzzy gloved paw.

It was Bay Area culture in the limelight.

Some fans arrived as early as 4 a.m. to claim spots along the rail. Some came from as far away as Concord, Pleasanton and Vallejo on the outskirts of the Bay Area. Others came from across the bridge. Others yet came from down the street. One fan flew from New York.

"Ballhalla is family," Valkyries fan Lie Crescini told the NBC broadcast. "There's 18,000 fans, and I like all of them. There's not one sibling I don't like in there."

Crescini lives in Oahu, Hawaii, but has not missed a single Valkyries game.

"This is what peace feels like. (Ballhalla is) loud, but it's peaceful."

As player buses slowly made their way down the Embarcadero, players got off to sign autographs, dance, take pictures and, in the case of center Aminata Gueye, hold dogs. Tiffany Hayes snatched a microphone from a reporter to work the crowd — "I'm married to (the game) now, I got me a ring" — before running across the street to greet fans in the spillover section. The crowd's energy never wavered, as marching bands, floats, cars, and buses filed past for about two hours, throwing beads and spraying bubbles.

The crowd was diverse and deep, and oozing with pride. The spirit of Ballhalla isn't confined to Chase Center — have Valks, Ballhalla will travel.

"We talk about so much, the different types of fans that the Valkyries attract, and it's the sports community, it's the LGBTQ community, it's young girls, it's families," NBC anchor Raj Mathai said. "… It's just the real sports fans and community activists here, and all that together makes the 18,000 fans strong at Chase Center."

This article originally appeared in The Athletic.

#2727. Billions quietly exchanged in major Mavericks ownership twist

A change of power has commenced in Dallas.

Sivan and Patrick Dumont are now in controlling power of the Mavericks after buying Mirian Adelson's shares in October, giving the family a 69% ownership share, ESPN reported Tuesday.

"It's really about long-term investment in the city of Dallas," Dumont told the outlet. "The Dumont family is really committed to building what we hope is the best arena in the NBA, a really significant investment in the city that will help create the new 40-year home for the Dallas Mavericks, a great experience for our fans and inspire our team to win championships. That's really what we're focused on. We had the opportunity, and we're really excited about it."

Dallas Mavericks owner Miriam Adelson, left, sits with daughter Sivan Ochshorn and governor Patrick Dumont during a game in Macao on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. The Dallas Morning News via Gett

Adelson, who had little involvement with the franchise despite her role, bought the majority share from Mark Cuban in December 2023 along with her daughter Sivan and son-in-law Patrick.

Thus, she still remains close to the team.

Cuban has since said he regretted selling after the Dumonts and Adelson pushed him out of the team's basketball and business operations side, but he still maintains a 27% share of the team.

Per the terms of the 2023 sale, Dumont has the option to buy another 20% share from the Shark Tank figure at the original $3.5 billion valuation.

Based on his comments, it's something the team governor plans to do.

"Our plan is to look at that and to do that over time," Dumont said. "I just have to tell you: I love Mark. He's been a great family friend for a really long time. He's just a super passionate Mavs fan and he's frustrated. I respect it. We're going to hopefully do him proud. That's my goal — to make all of our Mavs fans super proud about the success of the team and win a championship."

Dumont has issued various changes among the franchise during his tenure.

The Mavericks are expected to debut a new arena at the Valley View Mall in time for the 2031-32 season after calling American Airlines Center home since 2001. The team's practice facility and business offices are also undergoing renovations.

Dallas Mavericks governor Patrick Dumont watches play during the second half of an NBA game against the Golden State Warriors on Saturday, March 23, 2026. Getty Images

He is also tagged to the sudden trade of Luka Doncic, coming just months after the Mavericks' run to the 2024 NBA Finals. Dumont approved of former general manager Nico Harrison's decision to ship him to the Lakers — a bombshell trade that blew up the league overnight in February 2025.

The governor has since pivoted to put forth efforts in building around reigning Rookie of the Year, Cooper Flagg. After firing Harrison a year ago, former Raptors executive Masai Ujiri has all the power moving forward and has been given permission to make drastic changes.

"This is Masai Ujiri's team," Dumont said. "He's got a ring. He knows what he's doing."

The Mavericks are 4-3 heading into Wednesday's clash with the Spurs and will aim to make the playoffs after finishing just 26-56 last season.

The consistent theme and message about the 30-year-old forward has been his basketball IQ and filling in gaps that need to be covered on the floor with his off-ball movement and efficiency as a scorer. With the injury to superstar Anthony Edwards, Lyles will continue to see significant rotational action moving forward, getting minutes as both a backup forward, as well as filling in as a small-ball center — a lineup that Timberwolves head coach Chris Finch has not been hesitant to roll out in situations where he feels the team needs a spark.

"What I like about Trey is just a great, smart player. You know, makes things happen out there, is a really good help defender. Offensively, not only stretches the floor, but he's a good, like, next-action facilitator — really understands how to play basketball."

#2724. Game Preview: Suns get another shot at the team that started their season spiraling

Who: Phoenix Suns (1-4) vs. Portland Trail Blazers (5-1)

Where: Mortgage Matchup Center — Phoenix, Arizona

Watch: Arizona's Family 3TV, Arizona's Family Sports

The Suns are back at it on Wednesday evening as they return to the site of their only victory thus far this season. Home. What lies before them is a seven-game homestand, an opportunity to stabilize the front end of the season before things spiral into an unrecoverable tailspin.

Their opponent? The very team that sent them down this worrisome path in the first place, the Portland Trail Blazers, who led by as many as 52 points before handing Phoenix a 41-point defeat in the season opener.

In some respects, it feels like we're watching two teams heading in completely different directions. Last season, these teams met in the Play-In Tournament, with the Suns holding home-court advantage as the seventh seed. But the Trail Blazers, led by Deni Avdija, dispatched Phoenix with relative ease, putting the Suns in a position no team wants to find itself in. They were suddenly at risk of becoming the first seventh seed to miss the postseason entirely. Thankfully, Phoenix won its next game, earning a date with the Oklahoma City Thunder. We all know how that went.

But as this season has gotten underway, Portland has continued to build on the momentum it established a season ago, racing out to a 5-1 start. Meanwhile, the Suns find themselves on the opposite end of the spectrum at 1-4.

It's a small sample size, of course. At any point during an NBA season, a team can go 1-4 over a five-game stretch, and while there might be some concern, you probably don't think too much of it. But this is the foundation of the season. This is when we're getting to know what a team looks like, what it's capable of, what it does well, and where its opportunities for improvement lie.

When you look at the Portland Trail Blazers through that same lens, you see a roster constructed in a manner that makes sense, one capable of absorbing an injury or two without completely compromising its identity. That's exactly what they're dealing with. Ja Morant and Shaedon Sharpe are unavailable for this matchup, yet Portland possesses enough quality depth to remain competitive. Their absences don't necessarily derail what they're trying to accomplish.

The Suns, meanwhile, are experiencing something entirely different at the center position. Although Mark Williams is the only player listed as out on the injury report, his absence has created a ripple effect throughout the roster, one that becomes especially concerning when facing a team like Portland.

Perhaps Phoenix can use what happened in the season opener as motivation heading into Wednesday night. Nobody enjoys being embarrassed in the manner the Suns were, especially when the team responsible for that embarrassment is coming into your building. The question becomes: What are you going to do about it?

Mark Williams — OUT (Left Shoulder Surgery)

Jordan Goodwin — QUESTIONABLE (Right Calf Soreness)

Rasheer Fleming — QUESTIONABLE (Left Ankle Sprain)

Shaedon Sharpe — OUT (Right Meniscus Surgery)

The Suns' backcourt continues to be a point of evaluation for both the organization and the fan base. Jalen Green had what appeared to be a solid performance in the Suns' last outing, finishing with 11 points, eight rebounds, eight assists, and four turnovers. His playmaking abilities felt much more refined, although he certainly received some help from his friends, who were knocking down the shots he created for them.

The Suns' backcourt continues to be a point of evaluation for both the organization and the fan base. Jalen Green had what appeared to be a solid performance in the Suns' last outing, finishing with 11 points, eight rebounds, eight assists, and four turnovers. His playmaking abilities felt much more refined, although he certainly received some help from his friends, who were knocking down the shots he created for them.

Green finished the game with 11 potential assists, meaning his teammates failed to convert only three times when he put them in a position to score. That's a 73% conversion rate, which is pretty remarkable. Prior to Monday's game, his assist conversion rate was 48%.

But then you look at the other aspects of Green's game, and you can't help but wonder why he can't seem to put everything together at the same time.  He shot 1-of-6 from the free-throw line and 0-of-4 from beyond the arc, posting a true shooting percentage of 33.1%. Make a couple of those shots, and we're potentially talking about a much different outcome against Golden State.

So once again, I'll be watching how this backcourt performs, particularly whether Green can combine his improved playmaking with the scoring efficiency this team desperately needs.

I'll also be paying close attention to how Phoenix defends Portland, because the last time these teams met, the Suns were utterly atrocious on that end of the floor. You can chalk some of that up to it being the season opener, with players still trying to understand their assignments, responsibilities, and positioning within the defensive scheme. But regardless of the circumstances, Phoenix surrendered far too many wide-open three-pointers.

And Damian Lillard was more than happy to oblige, connecting on 6-of-10 attempts from beyond the arc.

Trail Blazers Shot Chart vs. Suns: 10/21/26 | hoopsjunkie.io

It's simple. This one comes down to rebounding. The Phoenix Suns are the worst rebounding team in the league by percentage, and they're going up against the best in the Portland Trail Blazers.

Phoenix has struggled mightily on the glass, both offensively and defensively. This roster doesn't have many players who can go up and simply snatch the shit out of the basketball. Instead, seemingly every rebound becomes an adventure in which poor positioning forces someone to tip the ball toward a teammate or desperately try to tap it back to themselves.

Meanwhile, Portland has long, rangy defenders who understand how to position themselves and secure rebounds, creating second-chance opportunities that can bury an opponent. It's something the Trail Blazers did well last season, and they're picking up right where they left off.

If the Suns want any chance of winning this game, they're going to have to earn every rebound through focus, positioning, and our good old friend, "give a shit".

There's nothing I've seen thus far this season that gives me confidence the Suns are going to win this game. They've been atrocious at defending the three-point line, their rebounding has been equally concerning, and those are two areas in which the Portland Trail Blazers have excelled early this season.

Perhaps this will be like last year, when everything came together in the fifth game. The defensive intensity started to manifest itself in a way that was both replicable and exciting to watch, giving us a glimpse of what this team could become.

I'd love to believe we're on the verge of witnessing something similar. I simply don't see it.

Treyton Harris has run for 1,058 yards and nine touchdowns. He also leads the defense with 72 tackles and has three sacks and two interceptions. Beckett Burton has thrown for 1,793 yards and 22 touchdowns. Brooks Johnson leads the defense with five sacks, and the Red Devils have 19 interceptions as a team.

The two teams' common opponents slightly favor Bountiful. Springville lost 38-35 at Alta, and Bountiful won there 29-28. Springville beat Olympus by 17, and Bountiful won 35-0.

To win on the road, Springville has to generate offense against a defense that hasn't allowed a point in three weeks. The Red Devils' offense has struggled at times. They scored nine points against Timpview and 14 against Orem. Harris needs to get going early so Burton isn't throwing into an aggressive Bountiful secondary that has scored three defensive touchdowns. Dave Valeti's team is trying to get back to the semifinals and beyond.

Bountiful's defense is playing as well as any in the state. The Redhawks have shut out their last three opponents: Brighton 38-0, Olympus 35-0 and Granger 47-0 in the first round. They have allowed 54 points in their last six games. They have won eight straight and won Region 6 outright at 5-0. Their only losses came in the first month against two of the best teams outside 5A, 25-14 at Herriman and 37-14 at Morgan. Both of those teams are still alive in the 6A and 3A playoffs. Bountiful also beat two 6A playoff teams, Farmington and Syracuse.

The secondary makes the most plays. Braden Boucha has four interceptions, two defensive touchdowns and a return touchdown. Mason Tidwell has four interceptions and a defensive touchdown, and on offense he averages 20.9 yards per catch with five touchdown catches. Jake Castlberry leads the team with 81 tackles. Manu Tia has 65 tackles and four sacks.

The offense was at its best against Granger. Hudson Malmrose threw four touchdown passes and ran for another, and Carter Brooks added a 59-yard touchdown run. Malmrose has completed 61.8% of his passes for 1,804 yards and 18 touchdowns. Max Feller is his top target, with 38 catches, 603 yards and seven touchdowns. Brooks leads the running game with 528 yards at 6 yards per carry. Bountiful averages 30.4 points per game, sixth in 5A.

The challenge is Springville's special teams and secondary. With Nadauld returning kicks and a defense that has 19 interceptions, Springville can score without a long drive. Bountiful has to win the field-position game. The last time these teams met in the quarterfinals, in 2023, Bountiful won 36-35 in overtime on a two-point conversion and went on to reach the title game. Jason Freckleton's team won the 5A championship a year later. Last season Bountiful lost 14-3 to West in this round. The winner plays the West–Fremont winner.

No one has found a way to slow West this season, and Fremont has to. The Panthers have outscored opponents 590-59. They have shut out their last four opponents and allowed 13 points in their last six games combined.

Fremont has faced better teams than most 5A clubs. It played two of the top teams in 6A, losing 56-28 to Davis and 49-0 at Corner Canyon. It also beat two 6A playoff teams, 34-3 over Weber and 14-11 at Farmington. The Silverwolves lost the Region 5 title by a single point, 17-16 to Box Elder. The two teams' only common opponent is Roy. Fremont won 55-8, and West won 63-0 in the first round.

Fremont is playing well right now. A month after losing 35-16 at West Field, it beat the Longhorns 43-23 in the first round. Calvin Cooper threw five touchdown passes in that game and ran for another. He has thrown for 1,969 yards and 21 touchdowns. Ky Majors leads the team with eight touchdown catches, and Breckon Phillips averages 20 yards per catch. Jak Masters leads the defense with 11 sacks, and Aisa Tuatagaloa has three interceptions and three sacks.

To pull the upset, Fremont has to keep the score low and limit West's big plays, especially on special teams. Lester Falatea has seven return touchdowns this season. Cooper has to protect the ball against a defense with 16 interceptions and 10 defensive touchdowns. Fremont also has to score on its few good chances, because West's defense won't give it many. The Silverwolves were upset in the quarterfinals last year as the No. 2 seed. This time they're the underdog.

For West, the plan is the same one that has worked all season. The Panthers lead 5A in scoring offense (53.6 ppg) and scoring defense (5.4 ppg). No opponent has scored more than 14 points against them. Their only close games were against out-of-state opponents, 20-14 over Arbor View (Nev.) and 21-13 over Archbishop Riordan (Calif.).

Kamden Lopati leads the offense. He has completed 69.6% of his passes for 2,831 yards and 28 touchdowns, with only four interceptions, and he averages 21.3 yards per completion. Naeata Hamilton has run for 872 yards and 12 touchdowns, and Derendrick Dixon has 15 total touchdowns.

Falatea may be the most dangerous player in the state. He has seven return touchdowns, including two punt returns against Roy. He also has six interceptions, three defensive touchdowns and two touchdown catches, for 12 total touchdowns. Takeshi Savery has 12 sacks and Dieter Lotulelei has 11, part of a 41-sack defense.

The challenge is the opponent. Fremont has been in more close games against good teams than anyone West has played. West's last game decided by fewer than five touchdowns was in August. Last year the Panthers lost 34-7 to Orem in the semifinals. Olosaa Solovi's team is chasing the school's first state title since 1992. The winner plays the Bountiful–Springville winner.

Pleasant Grove got even with one team last week, and it wants to do the same with another this week. In September the Vikings lost 28-24 at Spanish Fork when a late fumble rolled out of the end zone. Corbin Robbins ran for a touchdown and caught another, Cannon Jacobson threw two touchdown passes, and Davian Akwenye put the game away with a 55-yard interception return. Now the Vikings are back at Orem, where they lost 35-10 five weeks ago.

That game was closer than the score suggests. Pleasant Grove led 10-7 until Orem scored with 54 seconds left in the first half. After that, the Tigers scored 28 straight points. The Vikings need to play that first half again and then avoid the turnovers and stalled drives that let Orem take over.

Defense gives Pleasant Grove a chance. The Vikings allow 19.6 points per game, eighth in 5A. They have 23 interceptions and five defensive touchdowns, more of both than any team in these 5A previews. Jake Bills has five interceptions. Ethan Passey has four interceptions and a defensive touchdown. Akwenye has three interceptions, and all three became touchdowns. Clayton Lignell leads the team with 113 tackles, and Jaxon Mortenson has four sacks. Pleasant Grove has also beaten good teams outside its region, shutting out 6A Westlake 14-0 and winning 27-23 at 4A Green Canyon.

The Vikings need big plays to score. Robbins has 14 total touchdowns: eight rushing, two receiving, one on defense and three on returns. Ryder Huntsman has 54 catches for 670 yards. He has also thrown two touchdown passes and has two interceptions. Ben Lyman has made eight field goals. To win, Pleasant Grove has to protect the ball. Jacobson has thrown 10 interceptions, and Orem has scored five defensive touchdowns. A year ago Pleasant Grove lost in the first round. Jeremy Lapan's team has already won a road playoff game, and an upset of the defending champion would get it to the semifinals.

Orem needs to keep doing what has worked for seven straight weeks. The Tigers are the defending 5A champions. They've won seven straight since a 32-26 loss to Mater Dei (Calif.) in August and averaged 48 points over their last four games. Their only other loss was 21-14 at Skyridge, the 6A No. 1 seed. Orem allows 13.3 points per game, second in 5A behind West, and scores 35.5, third. It won Region 7 outright at 6-0.

The common opponents favor Orem. The Tigers beat Springville 42-14 and Spanish Fork 48-0. Pleasant Grove lost to Springville 34-8 and split with Spanish Fork. Orem also beat Maple Mountain 47-0 and Payson 55-28. Pleasant Grove's best result against a common opponent was a 28-21 win over Timpview, a team Orem beat by only three points in September.

Tanner Lewis threw five touchdown passes in last week's 55-7 first-round win over Timpview, four of them to Brooks Ross. Lewis has completed 62.5% of his passes for 1,480 yards and 20 touchdowns and has thrown one interception all season. Ross averages 18.1 yards per catch and has 11 touchdown catches. Po Faumui has 43 catches, seven touchdown catches and two defensive touchdowns. Beckham Curtis has run for 1,295 yards and 12 touchdowns at 8.8 yards per carry. Krew Jones, who scored twice in the first meeting, is a short-yardage option.

The defense has 33 sacks. Major Stokes has nine, Jag Ioane has eight and Jones has five. Kaio Akana has four interceptions and a defensive touchdown, and JaVoni Halalilo has two interceptions and two defensive scores.

Orem has to protect the ball against a defense that turns interceptions into points. Lewis has made that easy all season. In his first year at Orem, Andy Stokes is trying to lead the program to a second straight title. It would be Orem's ninth state title and sixth since 2017. Woods Cross nearly had its first-round win at Box Elder wrapped up. The Wildcats led through three quarters on two Sam Bahr touchdown runs and held the Region 5 champions scoreless. Then Box Elder came back in the fourth. Judd Howells ran 3 yards for a touchdown, Josh Pugsley returned a kickoff 94 yards, and Kadyn Reyes scored from the 1 on the final play of regulation to tie it. Tytan Hupp's 32-yard field goal put Box Elder ahead in overtime. Bahr answered with a 2-yard touchdown run, and the No. 14 seed won 29-26.

That's how Woods Cross has played all season. All five of its wins came by eight points or fewer: 27-26 over 6A Syracuse, 26-21 over West Field, 60-52 at Brighton, 36-35 over Viewmont and now Box Elder. Its losing record comes from a hard schedule. Five of its six losses came against playoff teams, including 4A seeds Stansbury and Snow Canyon.

The Wildcats nearly beat Alta six weeks ago, too. They led 7-6 going into the fourth quarter and were ahead again in the final minutes, until Lucas Pagel caught a 49-yard touchdown pass with 2:02 left. Xavier Cocci added a 15-yard run, and Tage Ita's 1-yard touchdown with 12 seconds left came too late.

Woods Cross wins by running the ball. Bahr has 11 rushing touchdowns, and he also has 60 tackles and an interception on defense. Ita has run for 522 yards and nine touchdowns and thrown for eight more. Bronson Martin averages 7.9 yards per carry, and Teiyon Halbasch averages 24.5 yards per catch. Abram Webre leads the defense with 95 tackles. Brody Rogers has six sacks and Napa'a Tuakiapimahu has five. Wyatt Hunter has two interceptions and a return touchdown.

To pull another upset, Woods Cross needs another close game in the fourth quarter. Ita also has to protect the ball. He has thrown 10 interceptions, and Alta's defense has 13 interceptions and five defensive touchdowns. Last year the Wildcats shared the Region 6 title and reached this round, losing 35-7 at Orem. Brody Benson, who won a state title at Highland in 2010, has them one win from the semifinals.

Alta's defense made Hillcrest's high-scoring offense look ordinary last week. Hillcrest came in averaging 39 points a game with a quarterback who had thrown 36 touchdown passes, and it scored seven in a 37-7 loss. After a scoreless first quarter, the Hawks scored 30 straight points in the second. Pagel ran for two touchdowns, Cocci threw a 12-yard touchdown pass to Ryland Clayton and ran 8 yards for another, and Hillcrest didn't score in the second half.

Alta has won three straight. It allows 17.8 points per game, seventh in 5A, and its defense has 34 sacks. Charlie Gates has 89 tackles and eight sacks, and Mason Albrecht and Kolt Handren have five sacks each. Thomas Deckart has 103 tackles, three interceptions and two defensive touchdowns. Mason Clark has 98 tackles and a defensive touchdown.

Alta also has the better schedule. It beat 5A quarterfinalist Springville 38-35, 6A Bingham 13-12 and Olympus 23-10. Its losses came against 6A quarterfinalists Davis (27-6) and Syracuse (28-7) and against Region 6 champion Bountiful, 29-28. Most common opponents favor the Hawks. Alta lost to Bountiful by one point, and Woods Cross lost 28-7. Alta beat Olympus by 13, while Woods Cross lost to the Titans 27-6. Alta also beat Viewmont and Brighton far more easily. Syracuse is the exception: it beat Alta by 21, and Woods Cross beat it by one.

Cocci leads the offense. He has thrown for 1,637 yards and 12 touchdowns, and he leads the team with 713 rushing yards and nine rushing touchdowns. Pagel has 11 total touchdowns: seven rushing, two receiving, one on defense and one on a return. Clayton averages 19.9 yards per catch and has five touchdown catches, plus two interceptions and a defensive score. Treven Cooke has 548 rushing yards. Madden McCallister has made seven field goals.

The concern is finishing. Woods Cross led Alta late in September and led Box Elder for most of last Friday, and the Wildcats don't go away. Alta lost in the second round last year. In his third season, Blake Burdette has the Hawks one win from their first semifinal since 2023, when they lost to Bountiful, and closer to the program's first state title since 2008. The winner plays the Orem–Pleasant Grove winner.

#2721. Hornets' Kon Knueppel to make season debut Wednesday vs. Nets following hamstring injury

Charlotte Hornets forward Kon Knueppel will make his season debut Wednesday against the Brooklyn Nets, the team announced.

The second-year sharpshooter has yet to play this season due to a strained left hamstring. Knueppel suffered the injury during "offseason on-court activity," the Hornets said in September. He sat out all of the preseason and the team's first eight games.

The 21-year-old Knueppel was initially listed as probable for the Nets game before receiving an upgrade in status hours before tip-off.

Last week, Knueppel was assigned to the team's G League affiliate in Greensboro, North Carolina, as part of his recovery.

Knueppel finished second in NBA Rookie of the Year balloting last season after challenging 2025 No. 1 overall pick and eventual winner Cooper Flagg by averaging 18.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.4 assists. Selected No. 4 overall out of Duke in the 2025 NBA Draft, he led the league by making 273 3-pointers and shooting 43% on 673 attempts.

He helped the Hornets improve to 44-38 and earn a spot in the NBA play-in tournament as the No. 9 seed, turning around from the league's third-worst record at 19-63 in 2024-25.

This season, Charlotte is off to a 3-5 start and have dropped four in a row heading into Wednesday's matchup in Brooklyn.

#2720. Joe Scarborough goes after ESPN’s Pat McAfee: ‘It is a shame for the viewer’

Pat McAfee is a problem for ESPN's "College GameDay," Joe Scarborough of "Morning Joe" hammered away at Tuesday during election day.

McAfee's recent headline-grabbing issues with the University of Utah was the tipping point.

"I've just had enough of this Pat McAfee ruining 'College GameDay,'" Scarborough said Tuesday. "I look forward to waking up on Saturday mornings and watching that. ... It's like he's melting down. ...

"It's really ESPN. I mean, they run their company the way they want to run their company, but man, it is a shame for the viewer."

McAfee revealed there have been death threats against him as a result of the controversy surrounding ESPN's "College GameDay" visit to Utah.

"I've stayed away from my mentions and DMs this month since these back to back days but ... I'm sure if I went in there now, I'd find some wishes for and threats of death for me," McAfee posted on X. "'Don't read them.' They're everywhere."

The post includes screenshots from direct messages threatening violence against him and tweets expressing a desire to see him dead.

The issue, according to Scarborough, is the show has gotten away from college football being played on Saturday and it's more about itself.

"I love watching Rece (Davis)," he said. "I love watching those guys and watching Nick (Saban) on there talking. ... Kirk Herbstreit's amazing. Desmond (Howard) — they're all great. And they're all being eclipsed by ESPN's just insatiable desire to give this guy more time."

"Maybe you aren't having to be yelling at people and being freaked out because two kids in Utah put up signs or say something that might offend you," Scarborough said.

Meanwhile, McAfee said he felt "uncomfortable" after the University of Utah posted a since-deleted video of students "dogging" him. He also said the video shared by the university account was inciteful against him.

McAfee cited the visit to the University of Utah reminded him of assassination of Charlie Kirk.

2 dead at Florida office complex, including gunman shot by security guardNov. 4, 2026, 5:44 p.m.

Second former NFL QB interviews for open NC State jobNov. 4, 2026, 2:33 p.m.

"I do get a bit (expletive) up when a couple days after The New York Times releases a 'WE ARE ALLOWED TO AND SHOULD HATE THIS GUY' piece, a university puts a video out from their own page, indicating, 'We think he's a corny creep here.' It's a weird time," McAfee posted. "The things that get said about what my daughter and son and wife deserve are all rather wild as well."

McAfee cited an experience ahead of "College GameDay" in Knoxville, Tennessee, in 2025 — the show's first episode after Kirk was killed.

He said security concerns arose about a potential "copycat" scenario, as "GameDay" was "the next huge gathering on a campus."

#2717. Mitchell Robinson is off to troubling Celtics start after bolting Knicks for $47 million deal

The grass hasn't been greener for Mitchell Robinson, even if his jersey is.

The former Knicks center is off to an inauspicious start with the rival Celtics after bolting in the offseason for a three-year, $47.4 million pact.

Robinson is averaging 6.2 points but just 4.4 rebounds and 0.7 blocks per game through six contests with a disastrous minus-42 rating when he's on the court.

Mitchell Robinson (4) of the Boston Celtics slam dunks against the Houston Rockets during a game in Houston, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. Getty Images

There has been speculation that the 7-foot, 240-pound big man reported to training camp in underwhelming physical shape, according to The Boston Globe.

"None of us have met the expectations, myself included," Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla said recently, per the outlet. "I have to be better, and it goes down the line. I like where Mitch is at from a mentality standpoint. I like his approach and his work ethic into doing the things that we're asking to do.

"It's obviously a little bit different, but none of us have met our own expectations, and we just have to keep working toward it. As long as we keep that mindset, not be distracted by the result, we got a chance. He's somebody that takes pride in that process of getting better, and I've enjoyed working with him."

The Knicks did not attempt to retain Robinson after he helped with the franchise's first title in 53 years in June and the Celtics swooped in to add some needed size to their frontcourt.

Six games is obviously an extremely small sample size, but there have been some worrisome signs.

Robinson posted a minus-16 rating in Monday's road loss to the Rockets and the Globe noted that he struggled on defense, "isn't moving as well as expected" and not contributing on offense.

Joe Mazzulla of the Boston Celtics high-fives Mitchell Robinson (4) during the first half against the Chicago Bulls on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, in Boston. Getty Images

His teammates reportedly are having "major trouble" finding him for alley-oops.

Robinson's points per game is actually slightly higher than his 2025-26 average, but his rebounds are notably down from 8.8 per game to 4.5 and his block have dipped from 1.2 to 0.7 per game.

The Celtics have a net rating of minus-18.8 when he's on the court compared to compared to plus-19.4 when he's off the court, per screwball.com.

The Knicks were better with Robinson on the court in each of the last two seasons per that metric, and his minus-38.2 net is the worst of his career.

"I would say for his offensive rebounding impact, we have him a little bit further away from the rim, setting screens and playmaking for us on the perimeter as part of our offense," Mazzulla said recently, per the Globe. "I think that has a little bit to do with it.

"But as far as the two-man game, it's just something to work on."

The Celtics have managed a 5-2 start despite Robinson's issues with their new system, and have a soft stretch coming up with three games against Milwaukee (twice) and Charlotte before a storyline-filled clash with ex-star Jaylen Brown and the 76ers next Tuesday.

#2715. The hits keep coming for wild-card hopefuls chasing the Packers

Heading into Week 9, the Green Bay Packers—and the rest of the NFC North—would make the NFL playoffs if the season ended now. Per the league's website, the NFL projects the Packers make the playoffs about half the time in simulations, with the Minnesota Vikings (81 percent), Chicago Bears (82 percent), and Detroit Lions (80 percent) well ahead.

Here's the good news: The Packers have a full-game lead over the next two teams breathing down their neck for the final wild-card spot, the Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams. On paper, it's a tight race between these teams, as the Seahawks are given a 47 percent chance of making the postseason, and the Rams are at 46 percent.

With how the landscape is playing out right now, the three wildcard spots in the NFC will likely all come down to North or West teams, and the South and East will just get one playoff team apiece. That means that two of Minnesota, Chicago, Detroit, Green Bay, Seattle or Los Angeles will be on the outside looking in at the end of the year.

Here's another bit of fortunate (I'll hesitate to call it good) news for the Packers, though: The Seahawks and Rams are banged up.

Already, it's been announced that Seattle quarterback Sam Darnold will miss next week's game against the Arizona Cardinals with a quad injury and is considered week-to-week. Darnold's backup, Drew Lock, is also dealing with an elbow injury. Per the NFL's projections, the Seahawks' chances of making the playoffs drop from 47 percent to 29 percent if they lose this weekend.

On the Rams' end of things, cornerback Jaylen Watson, their big $51 million free agent signing, will have shoulder surgery, as announced by head coach Sean McVay on Wednesday, and will not return this season. If, for whatever reason, they lose to the Washington Commanders, the Rams' playoff chances will drop from 46 percent to 31 percent.

Packers fans might not like it, but the team is firmly in the "already caring about the results of other teams' games" portion of the season — and honestly has been for a couple of weeks now. The Seahawks and Rams are the only legit threats to push Green Bay out of the postseason, at least for now, and there hasn't been a lot of positive news to come out about those clubs early on in Week 9.

#2712. Beware of the Lion – TSV 1860 Munich can still mix with the Bundesliga's best

MÜNCHEN (Bulinews): On our excursion to München last weekend, naturally topping the list of priorities was the Bundesliga's famed Der Klassiker as FC Bayern Munich hosted Borussia Dortmund on Saturday, 31 October. One could be forgiven for having tunnel vision.

To that, I would say do that at your own peril. The Friday prior to the bright lights of the Allianz Arena also served up a footballing delight in the vibrant southeastern suburb of Giesing. The might of TSV 1860 Munich taking on Regionalliga Bavaria rivals TSV Buchbach.

Four tier of German football you say? Fear not. A whopping 15,000 fans – of which maybe 1000 are Buchbach supporters – filter into the Grünwalder Stadion. The noise is already reaching fever pitch as we wind our way up the concrete steps of the South Stand.

Shortly after, the whistle blows to get the ball rolling. The football is nothing short of brilliant either. That blend of gritty 50-50 duels with no shirking out, coupled with some technical excellence. Namely, Buchbach's No.10 Tobias Heiland who neatly curled in the opening goal.

𝘋𝘪𝘦 𝘓ö𝘸𝘦𝘯 (The Lions) hit back in a flash. Ex-FC Augsburg star Florian Niederlechner and Felix Weber find the net. Still, Buchbach find a response. Heiland again with a sweet half-volley on the edge of the box before Samed Bahar's drive finds the bottom corner.

In need of a refreshment after a half that ended 3-2 to the guests, we make our way to the kiosk. As if the night couldn't get any more interesting, my colleague Manuel Veth of The Gegenpressing Podcast and I happen to bump into the referee's father there.

Overhearing some 1860 fans mulling over his son's first-half calls, he smiles but you sense a hint of paternal worry. The arbiter in question is 26-year-old Johannes Wagner – it was his first time officiating at this level. Might I add, he went on to do an exemplary job of it too.

Into the catacombs we go for an interval meeting with 1860 president Gernot Mang. There's no fancy murals or glitzy design to the interior. You must duck under the stand's support beams to avoid hitting your head. But that's football. Real football. I find it charming.

Mang is a charismatic, calmly spoken but passionate man who confesses his and the club's aim of returning to the Bundesliga – something they've missed since 2004. This isn't some crazed pipe dream. It's a mission. It may take time, but Giesing wasn't built in a day.

Back to our press box for the second helping of what seemed destined to be inevitable chaos. That's exactly what happens. Both sides had chances but Arian Calderon heads in from six yards for the hosts. We're tired at 3-3 with 8 minutes to play plus injury time.

With the clock hitting 90+4 minutes, space was afforded to Lance Fiedler. Buchbach stood off enabling the left-back to hammer a shot inside the left upright. Cue pandemonium in the terraces. You can't help but get caught up in it. Even the steward beside us delights.

Chants of "𝘌𝘪𝘯𝘮𝘢𝘭 𝘓ö𝘸𝘦, 𝘐𝘮𝘮𝘦𝘳 𝘓ö𝘸𝘦" (Once a Lion, forever a Lion) fill the cool Munich air. The three points sees them rise to second in the table. After the emotional rollercoaster, the party continues in Bamboleo – a 𝘒𝘯𝘦𝘪𝘱𝘦 – your unpretentious, cozy local matchday bar.

Sure, the allure of FC Bayern and BVB may have dominated the weekend. But in a way, the 1860 atmosphere is unfiltered and unmatched. One could argue it even surpasses their arch rivals in red and merits a hasty return to Germany's topflight.

Things may not be entirely harmonious behind the scenes after majority shareholder Hasan Ismaik's exit. However, the football drops jaws and the fans remain unwavering. A lion is the king of the jungle. It's fearless, resilient and untamable – TSV 1860 Munich embodies it all.

#2710. Next step? Fischer says Nets hope for big return for vets

The Nets rebuild can probably be traced back to June 25, 2024 when Brooklyn made two trades within minutes of each other that signals half steps were over. One sent Mikal Bridges to New York for five first rounders, a first round swap and a second rounder; the other an exchange of firsts with the Rockets that brought back a first rounder and a first round swap they had originally sent Houston in the first James Harden trade.

The second step was the two-year-long tank that helped the Nets get two high — although not as high as they had hoped — firsts in Egor Demin and Mikel Brown Jr. as well as five other late firsts. The hope, at least among fans, was that the losing or at least the deliberate losing would be over. Not yet, apparently, as Brooklyn is off to a 1-6 start and the two rookies have shared the court for only a few minutes. For the second straight year, the Nets are also the youngest team in the league, not a recipe for contention.

Now, into the fan caldron of disappointment, Jake Fischer seemingly dropped some knowledge that would seemingly ensure a longer rebuild. Speaking to Yahoo! Sports, the writer suggested that the next step could be trying to move veterans Michael Porter Jr and/or Julius Randle presumably at the February trade deadline, presumably to a contender, for more assets, presumably more picks or maybe other assets. Scoring, already an issue, and wins would be sacrificed.

"Brooklyn, I would still categorize as a team that is in more of a sell situation. I believe that Brooklyn will hope that a Julius Randle, a Michael Porter Jr. could still potentially draw some real returns," Fischer said.

"The Nets, they don't have their draft pick this year and they're looking to be better and compete in the Eastern Conference, take some strides forward in the East.

"I don't think they're going to be a full sell job right now, but I do think that they are still in a position to solicit trade offers for their veterans to get draft capital, potentially young pieces back in return."

Reading carefully, rather than scanning aggregators' headlines, reveals that Fischer isn't making predictions that the Nets will push hard to move both. He talks about "a Julius Randle," "a Michael Porter Jr." not both. Nor does he specifically mention the trade deadline. Nor does he gauge interest levels on the other side.

Adding to the Nets' cache of assets, of course, does make sense from a number of aspects. If, as Sean Marks has said, the ultimate goal is a player or players who will "automatically and absolutely change the trajectory of the franchise." then the accumulation of assets makes sense, particularly in an era where trades, not free agency, is the route to acquiring stars and superstars. Look at all the stars who moved this summer. Only LeBron James signed as a free agent and that of course was an oddity.

Either of the two players would seem to be the ideal final piece for teams hoping to make a final run at a title. Randle and MPJ can put up big numbers and have. Porter Jr. also has a ring. Yeah sure, both have baggage, but their ability to get buckets is undisputed. As Basket News noted,

Porter Jr. is averaging 20.7 points, 7.0 rebounds, 1.4 assists and 1.6 steals, shooting 38.1% from the three-point line.

In the meantime, Randle holds the averages of 20.9 points, 7.7 rebounds and 4.9 assists.

Their contracts also militate for moves unless the Nets see them as part of their future. MPJ will be an unrestricted free agent come July. If the Nets don't plan on extending him — and there's no indication at this point that they do, then trading him for assets in the interim would be imperative. Similarly, Randle has a player option at the end of this season and he too can leave in July if Sean Marks & co. decide not to make him an offer or an offer he believes fair. (MPJ earns $40.8 million, Randle $33.3 million with an option of $35.8 million.)

Of the two, Porter Jr. would seem to be the more likely to return assets. He's nearly four years younger than Randle, although Randle is closer to iron man status, having averaged 68 games a year over the last eight. He also has proven that he can be a leader during his time at Flatbush and Atlantic.

It should also be noted that any trade is unlikely to produce the automatic and absolute game-changer Marks has spoken about. More likely, it'd be the big trade before the bigger trade which might happen in the summer of 2027.

One of the most intriguing but also less than concrete suggestions in Fischer's comment is that the Nets might move away from accumulating draft picks to seeking "potentially young pieces" — that is, undervalued players on rookie deals. After all, they do have 13 firsts and 19 seconds over the next seven years. That strategy has been a key element in a number of recent rebuilds, most notably OKC's acquisition of a young Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, in the trade of Paul George to the Clippers back in June 2019. That one trade got Sam Presti one building block after another from SGA to Aday Mara. We should be so lucky.

Of course the trade deadline — 3:00 p.m. ET on February 11 — is three months away and there are few trades in the first couple of months of any season. The unofficial start of trade season is December 15 for two reasons. It's roughly 20 games into the season when teams understand what their needs are going forward as well as the first day that players signed or resigned during the off-season can be dealt. That expands the pool of players who are available by dozens. That's especially relevant putting together complicated, multi-team deals. Perhaps the spate of early season injuries will move things up, but it's unlikely.

#2709. Como hit nine in stunning Champions League win at Lens

Italian outfit Como equalled the record for the biggest winning margin in the modern Champions League with a stunning 9-1 victory away to Lens in France on Wednesday.

Greek international striker Anastasios Douvikas led the way with a hat-trick as the Serie A side, coached by Cesc Fabregas, claimed a third win in four games in this season's league phase.

Only two teams had previously won a game by a margin of eight goals since the launch of the modern UEFA Champions League in 1992.

Liverpool thumped Besiktas 8-0 in the group stage in 2007 and Real Madrid won by the same scoreline against Malmo in 2015.

Como are just the second team to score nine times in a game in the competition, after Bayern Munich beat Dinamo Zagreb 9-2 in the league phase in 2024.

According to statisticians Opta, the last club to score nine away from home was Feyenoord against Olympiacos in the old European Cup 1971.

Douvikas opened the scoring from close range in the seventh minute and finished again at the end of a superb team move just after the half-hour mark.

Argentine star Nico Paz rifled in to make it 3-0 at half-time, but Como really ran away with the game after the interval at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis in northern France.

Paz set up French international midfielder Lucas Da Cunha for 4-0, and Marc-Oliver Kempf headed in his team's fifth before Douvikas completed his hat-trick.

Mattia Liberali came off the bench and shortly after ran away to score the seventh, before Ruben Aguilar pulled one back for Lens with a fine volley.

However, Martin Baturina got Como's eighth in the 69th minute and Lens were lucky to concede only one more after that, as Matteo Papaccioli capped an incredible night for the visitors.

"There's nothing but positives for us to take this evening. Everything went right for us," said an understated Fabregas, as reported by UEFA.com.

Como, who finished fourth in Serie A last season to qualify for the Champions League for the first time, had already beaten both RB Leipzig and Manchester United 4-1 at home in this campaign.

They are fourth in the overall Champions League standings after four games with nine points, three points behind Paris Saint-Germain and Real Madrid, and one point behind Arsenal.

It is a third straight Champions League defeat for Lens and a record Champions League loss for a French club.

"It is hard to explain in the heat of the moment but the overriding feeling is one of humiliation," said their coach, Yannick Cahuzac.

#2708. 2026 NHL free agent tracker: Patrick Kane returns to Blackhawks on two-year contract

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NHL free agency has slowed down in late July, but some notable names are still coming off the board. Most notably, Patrick Kane is returning to the Chicago Blackhawks on a two-year contract worth $16 million, the team announced on Thursday.

Already a Chicago legend and future Hall of Famer, Kane won three Stanley Cups and a slew of individual awards with the franchise that selected him with the No. 1 overall pick in 2007. Kane's first stint with the Blackhawks lasted 16 seasons, and he piled up 446 goals and 779 assists in 1,161 games. Kane ranks inside the top five of just about every statistical category in franchise history, and he will get the chance to keep climbing those lists over the next two years.

The Blackhawks sent Kane to the New York Rangers at the 2023 NHL trade deadline, and he played just 19 regular season games there before hitting free agency the next summer. Hip surgery delayed Kane's decision until November of that year, but he ultimately landed with the Detroit Red Wings, where he's spent the last three seasons.

Last season was Kane's best with Detroit, and it proved that he still had some gas left in the tank, at least offensively. Kane posted 16 goals and 41 assists in 67 games -- with 19 of those points coming on the power play.

In his second stint with the Blackhawks, Kane will add another level of playmaking to the power play, and he should strengthen a top six forward group that's bereft of proven talent. Kane will also be an excellent mentor and sounding board for fellow No. 1 overall pick, Connor Bedard, who is set to miss the first month of the season after undergoing shoulder surgery.

Kane isn't the player he once was, but he'll give Chicago a bit more pop at the top of the lineup, and his first game back in a Blackhawks jersey will be a huge night for the city.

#2707. Former Steelers RB Merril Hoge joins in praise of Mike McCarthy

The Pittsburgh Steelers are 6-2 and in prime position to win the AFC North in back-to-back seasons.

Aaron Rodgers has turned back the clock and is playing at a solid level, leading the Steelers offense to four consecutive victories. People didn't know what to expect with Mike Tomlin out of the picture and Pittsburgh's own Mike McCarthy taking over. More of the same? A better-executed offense? The first losing season in over two decades? So far, so good.

Apologies and credit where credit is due have been the main theme of the bye week for many in the media who were wrong, at least to this point, about the 6-2 team. NFL analyst and former offensive guard Damien Woody is surprised by how McCarthy has anchored the veteran team.

"I have to admit, I did not envision the Pittsburgh Steelers playing as well as they're playing so far as we approach the halfway point," Woody said on The OG Football Show. "I got to give my flowers to Mike McCarthy."

The Steelers offense ranks 13th in total yards per game (351.8) and 14th in rushing (117.9). After years of failing to run the football, McCarthy and offensive line coach James Campen are delivering a legitimate running game.

"Mike McCarthy has done a hell of a job," Woody said. "People frown upon him, but all Mike McCarthy has done is win in Green Bay; he won in Dallas, and now in his first year in Pittsburgh he has them sitting atop the AFC North… Mike McCarthy, Aaron Rodgers and company are pushing all the right buttons. Former Steeler and current broadcaster Merril Hoge believes the Super Bowl champion coach belongs in Canton for his decades of success in three cities.

"If you took his resume and his credentials and stacked it up to Hall of Famers, it's very similar and better in some ways," Hoge said. "He gets no credit for that. Nobody thinks of him like that. The Steelers are exceeding expectations, and historically, 90% of teams that start 6-2 make the playoffs. Are the pieces coming together to make a playoff run for the first time in a full decade?

Former Cowboys wide receiver Dez Bryant is already looking ahead. He has picked out his choice to be the next head coach.

Posting on X, Bryant stated: "I'm just saying… if anything were to happen in Dallas…Jason Witten should be the next head coach of the Dallas Cowboys. I can see it..and I'd love that."

Jason Witten was Bryant's teammate on the Cowboys for eight seasons between 2010 and 2017. It certainly makes sense that he would love to see his former colleague play his role in rejuvenating the franchise.

Since his retirement from the NFL after the 2020 season, Witten has moved into coaching. But he is still early in his career.

Witten became head coach at Liberty Christian School, where he led them to win back-to-back TAPPS state championships in 2023 and 2024, including the school's first-ever TAPPS Division I title.

He made a new step earlier this year when he was named tight ends coach for the Oklahoma Sooners.

Just this month, Witten has been named as the Sooners' offensive coordinator, after Ben Arbuckle was fired.

While Jerry Jones could certainly be swayed by a great story in bringing Witten home to Dallas, it certainly seems like a huge jump right now. Witten himself would rather continue to learn the ropes in college football.

If Brian Schottenheimer can somehow extend his run with the Cowboys by another three or four years, Witten may end up as his successor.

But if their current trajectory continues, the Cowboys may need a replacement for Schottenheimer in January 2027 – and that may rule Witten out.

#2702. For today and tomorrow, Labaron Philion needs more minutes

The Sixers are 7-1 after Monday night's 126-107 victory against Chicago. Three of their next four games are against fellow Eastern Conference contenders in Detroit, Cleveland and Boston. Perhaps for that reason, Nick Nurse might not make drastic changes to a rotation that keeps winning. After all, the Sixers haven't opened a playoff round at home since 2023 so locking up wins against other teams in the Eastern Conference now can only help for seeding later. However, there's one glaring mistake with Nurse's rotation that he needs to address.

When it comes to the bench, Nurse is playing Anfernee Simons, Dean Wade and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope regularly. These are veterans who figure to factor into the playoff rotation as well come the spring. However, whether Labaron Philon sees the court in April and beyond or not, the rookie out of Alabama should be seeing more than the eight minutes per game he's currently averaging. Even in a 19-point win against the Bulls, Philon played just two minutes.

While Philon was drafted towards the end of the first round this past summer, now's the time to find out what kind of player he could become. Of course, he can always grow into a bigger role next season and beyond, but should the Sixers set him on a path that's essentially burning a year of his rookie contract? Maybe that's a harsh way of phrasing things after only eight games, but it's the realest way of saying Philon isn't playing nearly enough.

For context, Tyrese Maxey was drafted 21st overall in 2020 which is just one spot earlier than Philon's 22nd overall in 2026. In the 2020-21 season, Maxey's rookie year, Maxey played 15 minutes per game and started eight games. That's a considerable uptick from the amount of minutes Philon is currently playing. Additionally, under Nick Nurse in 2024-25, Jared McCain played 25.7 minutes per game as a rookie in an injury-shortened season that saw him still start eight games. Neither of these comparisons is perfect as McCain was nearly a lottery pick having been selected 15th overall in 2024 and Maxey would have probably been a lottery pick under non-COVID circumstances in his draft eligible season in college.

Part of the reason we're saying the Sixers have a backup center problem yet again is because they whiffed on the Johni Broome pick recently and Adem Bona doesn't seem to have any offensive skillset. Granted, those two players were recent second-rounders by Philadelphia, but the point stands. You want to get your draft picks on the court in their rookie seasons in the regular season when your rotation should be deeper. It's cheap production if they're good right away, gives you more clarity on what they could develop into down the line, and would also make it easier to move off of them in trades while they still have some trade value if the early returns aren't to your liking.

In the short term, don't we all agree Maxey could use more of a breather than what he's currently getting? Maxey is averaging a whopping 37.4 minutes per game which is currently second in the NBA to only Denver's Jamal Murray. Maxey's injury history is nowhere near as lengthy as Joel Embiid's, but that doesn't mean Maxey wouldn't benefit from seeing his minutes scaled back a bit. Maxey's also doesn't seem like the kind of player that would be concerned about various individual accolades that might not come his way if his playing time decreased. More importantly, everyone can agree Maxey needs to be healthy and full go come playoff time for Philadelphia to make a deep run.

In the long term, wouldn't it be great if Philon developed into a sixth man at the very least for this team? Remember how awful Philly's bench was in the playoffs last year? Philon represents a long-term solution to what's been a long-term problem for the Sixers even if it's hard to see him ever getting on the court with long-term building blocks in Maxey, VJ Edgecombe and Jaylen Brown all at the same time.

Make no mistake, winning is fun and the Sixers are doing a lot of it right now. But the best teams in every sport can fuse the present with the future and win in the current season and in seasons of tomorrow. I get it Sixers fans, the current season is probably all that's on your mind and I can't blame you as the Sixers have as good a chance as any other team does to win the NBA championship in 2026-27. But there's going to be basketball played in 2027 and beyond and Labaron Philon was drafted to be a part of that basketball for Philly so this season should also be about finding out what role Philon can have within this organization's long-term plans.

Few things drive athletes to greatness as much as a chip on their shoulder, and Golden State Valkyries center Kiah Stokes showed that off Wednesday at the team's WNBA championship parade.

Stokes arrived at the Golden State parade down San Francisco's Embarcadero sporting a T-shirt with ESPN's WNBA BPI, or basketball power index. The shirt refers to ESPN Analytics' July 26 ranking of which teams had the best chances to win the 2026 WNBA title. The Indiana Fever ranked No. 1, with a 24% chance, followed by the Las Vegas Aces, Minnesota Lynx, New York Liberty and Atlanta Dream. Conspicuously absent, of course, were the Valkyries.

The Valkyries clinched their first WNBA title on Saturday with a Game 7 win over the Dream. Stokes came ready to celebrate on Wednesday, spraying sparkling wine over the fans who lined the Embarcadero to cheer on the team. Stokes is no stranger to success; this is her fourth WNBA championship. She won her first three with the Aces in 2022, 2023 and 2025.

ESPN Insights, the home of ESPN's analytics division, posted a mea culpa on X on Wednesday. "Golden State was 6th on the leaderboard when we posted it on July 26, but went 13-4 from there!" the post read. "ESPN Analytics had the Valkyries as title favorites by August 10. Sorry we were a little late to the party."

If you're hoping to grab the shirt, it does appear to be a custom-made design. But perhaps Stokes could stand up a merchandise business, as Valkyries fans undoubtedly wouldn't mind the chance to buy their own.

#2700. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#2696. Dumont family takes full control of Mavericks, buying Miriam Adelson's shares

Patrick and Sivan Dumont have formally become the controlling owners of the Dallas Mavericks after purchasing Miriam Adelson's shares of the franchise last month, a story broken by Tim MacMahon of ESPN. The Dumonts now own 69% of the Mavericks.

While this is a change at the top, it should have little day-to-day impact, as Patrick Dumont has served as team governor and been the acting owner on the ground since the day Mark Cuban sold the team to the Dumonts and Adelsons. Here is what Dumont told ESPN:

"It's really about long-term investment in the city of Dallas," Dumont told ESPN on Tuesday. "The Dumont family is really committed to building what we hope is the best arena in the NBA, a really significant investment in the city that will help create the new 40-year home for the Dallas Mavericks, a great experience for our fans and inspire our team to win championships. That's really what we're focused on. We had the opportunity, and we're really excited about it."

As Cuban said when he sold his majority share of the team, the NBA has become a real estate business, and what Dumont is looking to build is not just a new arena but the anchor of a much larger development. That is the trend with professional sports franchises in general, including the Dallas Cowboys.

Dumont, the Las Vegas Sands Co. CEO, has experience with building and development. He didn't have experience as an NBA owner when he took over the team, and that position comes with a learning curve (a longer one for some than others). Dumont became a villain early in his ownership of the Mavericks when he approved the controversial trade of Luka Doncic to the Lakers, which led to severe backlash from fans in Dallas. Dumont told ESPN's MacMahon he learned from those experiences.

"The most important thing every day is just trying to work harder to get better," Dumont said. "It's something that really applies in life, but it's something that really applies to here. It's been an experience as a new owner in the league. Dallas is a great sports city. I think we have the best fans in the NBA, very passionate, and it's my job to make sure that we win and that we support our fans. I'm really focused on that. I've learned that there are a lot of things you can do -- sometimes they work, sometimes they don't -- but you've got to keep pushing, got to keep going."

Dumont made changes in the front office, bringing in Masai Ujiri to run the show, then Ujiri fired coach Jason Kidd to bring in Dusty May. Dumont spent millions to upgrade the team's practice facilities. All of this with the idea of trying to maximize the team around Cooper Flagg, who in his second NBA season is looking elite and like an All-NBA player already. The new arena will ultimately be remembered as the one Cooper built.

#2694. Kellen Moore confirms Charlie Smyth will kick for the Saints this week

The Saints released veteran kicker Daniel Carlson on Tuesday. Coach Kellen Moore confirmed Wednesday that Charlie Smyth will kick for them this week.

"Yeah, Charlie will kick this week," Moore said, via video from the team. "Tough decisions. Daniel, he's made some really good kicks for us. I think just the consistency thing. Just felt like this was the best thing for our football team moving forward. These things are never easy, but Charlie's done this for us back in the last year, so he'll be ready to go."

In his first season with New Orleans, Carlson made just 8-of-12 field goals in seven games. All four misses came on attempts of at least 50 yards. He missed a 52-yard attempt during the fourth quarter of the Saints' Week 7 loss to the Steelers in Paris.

Smyth, a native of Northern Ireland, went 12-of-16 on field goals in six games for the Saints in 2025.
